claims.text: Combining ab initio-trained machine-learned interatomic potentials with enhanced sampling will preserve full free-energy fidelity.
The proposed method will retain vibrational-entropy, anharmonic, and electron–vibration-coupling contributions.
The proposed method will reduce the cost of fusion-property calculations for multicomponent high-entropy systems relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost relative to TOR-TILD.
The enhanced free-energy scheme will explicitly account for anharmonic effects.
The enhanced free-energy scheme will explicitly account for electron–vibration effects.
The intended operating range is within approximately 100 K of the melting point.
Free-energy accuracy is mediated by the MLIP's ability to reproduce the anharmonic potential-energy surface.
Free-energy accuracy is mediated by the MLIP's ability to reproduce explicit electron–vibration coupling.
The training dataset controls the MLIP's ability to reproduce the relevant free-energy landscape.
The enhanced-sampling method's ability to capture rare events controls the accuracy of the free-energy landscape.
Replacing on-the-fly ab initio force calculations with MLIP evaluations will dramatically reduce CPU time.
Enhanced sampling will accelerate phase-space sampling without sacrificing the accuracy needed to resolve subtle entropy contributions.
Prior success in elemental and binary systems provides a basis for extending the approach to high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method will produce free energies within 50 meV per atom of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The proposed method will predict fusion temperatures within 50 K of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by approximately one order of magnitude.
Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD accurately capture free energies in elemental and binary systems.
Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD become prohibitively expensive or slow for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The method is expected to remain valid for systems containing five or more principal components.
